newsitem.title: USA: J.C. Penney offers early retirement to 1,500.
newsitem.headline: J.C. Penney offers early retirement to 1,500.

text.p: J.C. Penney Co. Inc. said Monday it will offer voluntary early retirement to about 1,500 people, or 5 percent of its management staff, in a bid to cut costs to compensate for recent weak profits.
The retail giant said the package would reduce costs by $120 million a year if accepted by all of the eligible managers, and may reduce the need for additional staff cuts in the future.

Chairman James Oesterreicher said J.C. Penney would post a one-time, pretax charge of up to $200 million later this year for the early retirement programme, with the exact charge depending on how many of the employees take the buyout.

"We recognise that in order to continue to build on our leadership position in an increasingly competitive retailing environment, it is essential for us to continue to develop a competitive cost structure," he said in a statement.

"We are firmly committed to accelerating our ongoing expense reduction programme and significantly lowering our expense-to-sales ratio. We will increase our operating efficiencies, work on process changes and implement additional cost-saving initiatives," he added.
J.C. Penney has about 250,000 employees in all.

The early retirement will be offered to management associates at all J.C. Penney stores, its catalogue business and in corporate offices if they are or will be 55 years old and have at least 10 years of service with the company as of April 10, 1998.
Employees of the company's Eckerd drugstores, which it bought earlier this year in a deal valued at $3.3 billion, and at its insurance subsidiaries are not eligible for the programme.
One of the nation's leading department store chains, J.C. Penney has struggled lately under the weight of weak sales and excess inventories.

"We have been less than satisifed with our results in the past year," Chief Financial Officer Donald McKay said in a telephone interview. ""We have taken a series of measures to address that and we have a positive view going forward."
Penney is expected to report its second-quarter results Tuesday, and most analysts expect earnings per share to stay flat at around 37 cents.
McKay declined to comment on J.C. Penney's revenue outlook for the months ahead but said the company hoped a new advertising campaign and a series of other measures would boost sales.
"It is a very competitive business, and we want to stay competitive," he said.
David Poneman, an industry analyst with Sanford C. Bernstein and Co. Inc., said he expects J.C. Penney will take further cost-cutting steps in the months ahead.

"I don't think this is the last we will hear," Poneman said. "This is something Penney has to maintain a real focus on given that they haven't been fully satisfied with their results over the last couple of years."

Even as J.C. Penney's department store sales have shown sluggish growth, the company has focused on expanding its pharmacy business, culminating with the acquisition of Eckerd Corp., the No. 4 drug store chain in the United States.
Monday's buyout news was released after the close of trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where the company's stock rose 50 cents to close at $58.125.
